name: Levels of processing
statement: What a person does with material at study, rather than how long or how hard they work at it, determines how much of it they later remember.
meaning: Two claims travel under this name and they are not equally well supported. The first is an experimental result. Judge a word for its meaning and you will recognise it later; judge the same word for its typeface and you will not. The second is the framework Craik and Lockhart built around that result: perception runs through levels from surface features to meaning, the memory trace is a by-product of however far that analysis got, and trace persistence rises with depth. The framework carries three further commitments that the effect itself does not need. Repeating an analysis at one level should buy nothing. Deeper traces should decay more slowly. And depth should be an independent property of the encoding, not a label read backwards off the memory score. Each of the three has been tested. The result holds; the commitments have fared worse, and the authors withdrew several of them within three years.

origin.who: Fergus I. M. Craik and Robert S. Lockhart
origin.where: Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior
origin.note: The paper reports no experiments. It reviews the case for multistore models of memory, argues that their inconsistencies are better handled by looking at encoding operations, and proposes depth as the organising variable. Its own summary of its status is flat: the approach "does not constitute a theory of memory" but offers "a set of orienting attitudes". Craik and Lockhart also conceded on the page that "spread" would describe their idea more accurately than "depth", and kept "depth" because it "conveys the flavor of our argument".

evidence: The demonstration everyone cites is Craik and Tulving's ten experiments of 1975, run at Toronto and framed to subjects as a study of perception. In Experiment 1, 20 paid college students saw 40 words in a tachistoscope, each preceded by one of five questions. Is a word present, is it in capital letters, does it rhyme with a given word, is it in a given category, would it fit a given sentence frame. An unexpected recognition test followed, 40 targets among 40 distractors. Recognition of words answered yes ran .22, .18, .78, .93 and .96 across those five questions, and words answered no ran .14, .36, .63 and .83. Median decision latencies climbed with the question, 591 to 746 ms for yes responses, F(4, 171) = 35.4, p < .001, and the recognition effect of question type was F(3, 133) = 52.8, p < .001. Craik and Tulving put the mismatch plainly: 200 msec of extra study time led to a 400% improvement in retention. Experiment 2 tightened the design with 24 subjects, three question types and 120 distractors. Recognition of yes words rose from 15% after a typescript question to 81% after a sentence question, F(2, 46) = 118, p < .001; no words rose from 19% to 49%. Experiment 5 is the one that decides between depth and time. A shallow task, judging whether a word matched a consonant-vowel pattern such as CCVVC, took 1.70 and 1.74 sec against .83 and .88 sec for the sentence task, and it produced worse recognition, .57 and .50 against .82 and .69, F(1, 23) = 40.9, p < .001. A slow shallow task loses to a fast deep one. The experiments also turned up something the framework did not predict. Words that fitted their question were remembered better than words that did not, .93 against .63 for category questions, although yes and no decisions took the same time. Craik and Tulving read this as elaboration rather than depth, and it is why the 1975 paper introduces congruity as a separate factor.

replication.headline: Peng, Logie and Della Sala found deep encoding ahead of shallow on immediate recognition in all three of their experiments, partial eta squared 0.34 to 0.57, with 86, 72 and 114 participants.
replication.detail: The three experiments were run online in two sessions, with recognition tested immediately and again after a delay. Experiment 1 set semantic judgements against rhyme judgements in 86 participants after exclusions, and immediate recognition gave d prime 2.61 for deep against 2.10 for shallow, F(1, 83) = 49.24, p < .001, partial eta squared 0.37. Experiment 2 used the consonant-vowel task from Craik and Tulving's Experiment 5 with 72 participants, and the shallow task again took longer to perform, 3,774 ms against 2,912 ms, while producing worse memory: d prime 1.83 against 2.58, F(1, 66) = 87.43, p < .001, partial eta squared 0.57. Experiment 3 moved the manipulation between participants, 114 after exclusions, and gave 2.11 against 2.83, F(1, 108) = 55.45, p < .001, partial eta squared 0.34. The advantage survived every delay tested, from 30 minutes to 24 hours, with delayed-recognition effects of partial eta squared 0.25 to 0.35. Its shape did not change with delay. No experiment found a levels by delay interaction, and the Bayes factors favoured the null at 6.57, 5.76 and 3.21. Fitting power functions to the retention curves gave no difference between the forgetting slopes of deep and shallow items, chi-squared(1) = 2.25, p = .134 in Experiment 1 and chi-squared(1) = 1.26, p = .262 in Experiment 2. The authors conclude that rates of forgetting are independent of the encoding operations levels of processing manipulates. No multi-site or registered replication of the effect was located; the searches covered Crossref, Europe PMC and general web search.

study.cite: Peng, N., Logie, R. H., & Della Sala, S. (2025). Effect of levels-of-processing on rates of forgetting. Memory & Cognition, 53(2), 692-709.

limits: The effect is robust and the framework around it is not, which makes the boundary between them the thing worth knowing. Craik and Lockhart proposed that deeper analysis leaves a longer lasting trace. Peng, Logie and Della Sala tested that directly and found parallel forgetting curves: depth sets how much is learned and does nothing to how fast it goes. The framework also held that repeating an analysis at the same level, what Craik and Lockhart called Type I processing, "does nothing to enhance memory for the stimulus". Two 1977 papers reported otherwise. Nelson's three experiments found that repetition at the phonemic level does help, whether massed or distributed and whether the measure is uncued recall, cued recall or recognition. Glenberg, Smith and Green isolated Type I rehearsal and found that more of it improved recognition, concluding that it "serves more than a maintenance-only function". The strongest empirical objection is Morris, Bransford and Franks. Semantic study beat rhyme study on an ordinary recognition test, and rhyme study beat semantic study when the test asked which words rhymed with a probe. Depth is therefore not a property of encoding alone but of the fit between encoding and test, which is the transfer-appropriate processing account. Craik reports that averaged over their first two experiments the semantic study with semantic test combination still reached 0.68, against 0.40 for rhyme with rhyme. Those two figures are quoted here from his description of that paper, which is paywalled, and not from the paper. Craik and Tulving themselves withdrew much of the 1972 apparatus in the same paper that is cited as its confirmation. They abandoned the fixed series of analysers, abandoned decision time as an index of depth, and wrote that "differential depth of encoding does not seem a promising description, except in very general terms" and that many of the 1972 ideas "stand in need of considerable modification". Craik later conceded a further boundary: amnesic patients understand what they are told and still do not remember it, so "deep processing is necessary but not sufficient for later episodic memory".
misreadings: The circularity objection is the one most often garbled. It is normally credited to Baddeley's 1978 paper in Psychological Review, and it does not say the effect is false. It says that without a measure of depth taken independently of memory, the framework cannot be wrong: whatever is well remembered can be relabelled as deeply processed. Craik states it in that form himself and accepts it, writing that the absence of an objective index of depth is a major criticism and that psychology is "stuck for the moment with such unsatisfactory methods as agreement among judges". His own attempted index, decision time, fails in both directions. It fails within the 1975 data, where yes and no decisions took equal time and produced unequal memory, and it fails across materials, because an expert encodes material in their field quickly and remembers it well. Baddeley's paper is paywalled, and the statement of the objection quoted here is Craik's restatement of it, not Baddeley's wording. A second error treats levels of processing as a theory that was tested and beaten. Craik and Lockhart said in the paper that it was not a theory, and its main empirical prediction keeps coming out right. A third error reads depth as effort or as time on task. Craik and Tulving's list of what does not determine retention is explicit: not intention to learn, not the amount of effort, not the difficulty of the task, not the time spent judging, not even the amount of rehearsal. Their Experiment 5 is built to make the point, and Peng and colleagues rebuilt it with the same result. A fourth error is that the effect needs incidental learning, on the reasoning that a subject who knows about the test will process everything deeply. Craik and Tulving got the same pattern under intentional learning in Experiments 4 and 9, and every participant in the 2025 replication was told about the memory test in advance. The last error is quoting the .96 from the 1975 paper as the depth effect. That figure is a sentence question answered yes, and congruity between question and word is a separate factor doing part of the work; the matching no cell is .83, and at the category level the gap is .93 against .63.
